title: The pale blue dot
hook: a 1990 photograph from Voyager 1 shows Earth as a speck in a sunbeam

segments.voice: Yesterday Marcus rose above the city in his mind: the view from above. Your line was so small, so loved. Did a big worry shrink, even for a breath? Day one hundred twenty-three.

Marcus had to imagine the view from above. In 1990, we got to see it. A small spacecraft called Voyager 1 had been flying away from Earth since 1977. It had passed Jupiter and Saturn, and was heading out of the solar system forever. Its cameras were about to be switched off to save power. Before they were, the astronomer Carl Sagan and his colleagues persuaded NASA to do something with no scientific purpose at all: turn the camera around, and take one last picture of home. Today: the pale blue dot.
screen: `VOYAGER 1, SINCE 1977.` → `LEAVING THE SOLAR SYSTEM.` → `TURN AROUND. ONE LAST PICTURE.`

segments.voice: On February 14, 1990, from about six billion kilometers away, nearly four billion miles, Voyager 1 took a series of pictures of the planets. In one of them, there's a band of scattered sunlight across the frame, and sitting in it, a single tiny dot, less than one pixel wide. That dot is Earth. Every ocean, every city, every person alive in 1990, inside a speck you could miss if a hair landed on the photo. Sagan wrote about it a few years later, in his book Pale Blue Dot. His words are too recent to quote here, but in our own words, the heart of them is this: that little dot is us. Every person you have loved, every name in every history book, every ruler and every farmer, every parent singing a child to sleep, the whole human story, happened on that speck of dust floating in a beam of light. And he drew two lessons from it. First, humility: all our pride, our wars over who rules a fraction of the dot, look very small from out there. Second, responsibility: as far as we know, this speck is our only home, and nobody else is coming to fix it for us. So it's on us to treat each other better, and take care of the place. It's Marcus's view from above, made real. Same two halves. So small. So loved. Everyone, all of us, on one speck.
screen: `FEBRUARY 14, 1990.` · `LESS THAN ONE PIXEL.` · `EVERYONE WHO EVER LIVED, THERE.` · `HUMILITY, THEN RESPONSIBILITY.` · then, large: `EVERYONE ON ONE SPECK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at the photo for a minute. After the bell, you can find it by searching pale blue dot. For now, picture it. A dark field. A slanting band of light. And in it, one pale dot. Hold it in your mind. Now remember, one at a time: someone you love is on it. Someone you're angry with is on it. You are on it. Everyone who ever lived. Rest your attention on the dot, and breathe. The bell holds the time.
The pale blue dot. Earth, photographed by Voyager 1 in 1990, a speck in a sunbeam holding everyone. Today's word.
Your line: everyone on one speck. Today, when someone annoys you, a driver, a stranger online, remember the dot: they're on it too, the only home either of you has. Day one hundred twenty-three.

howItsDone: Many people, religious and not, keep the Pale Blue Dot photograph as a reminder of scale, and teachers, scientists and faith leaders alike use it to talk about humility and care for the earth.

fork.setup: you run the Voyager mission. the cameras are about to be shut off to save power. an astronomer asks you to turn the spacecraft around for one picture of Earth, with no scientific use. what do you do?
options: refuse: it's a waste of the mission.
turn it around and take the picture.
take a picture of another planet instead.
fork.reveal: after some persuading, NASA turned Voyager 1 around on February 14, 1990. the result became one of the most famous photographs ever taken.

trapdoor: what you thought: a cool space photo.
what it means: every person who ever lived, inside a speck less than a pixel wide, and a reason for humility and care.
what a scholar hears: part of the Family Portrait, a mosaic of about sixty frames, the last images Voyager 1 took before its cameras went dark.

sources.ref: Voyager 1 Pale Blue Dot image, February 14, 1990 (NASA/JPL)
Carl Sagan, Pale Blue Dot: A Vision of the Human Future in Space (1994), chapter 1

notes: Sagan's 1994 passage is under copyright and is paraphrased only, in deliberately different wording; the 'responsibility' paraphrase (no sign help will come from elsewhere; be kinder to one another) follows his argument closely, so a Keeper should check it reads as paraphrase, not quotation.

Facts to confirm: February 14, 1990; about 6 billion km (3.7 billion miles); Earth about 0.12 pixel; Family Portrait of about 60 frames; these were Voyager 1's last images; Voyager 1 launched in 1977.
'No scientific purpose' is a common description; some at NASA saw minor value. Confirm framing.
